paras: The threatened lynching of John Davis took place in Stamford in late July or early August 1882, when friends of women and girls he was accused of trying to assault lay in wait to lynch him. Officers arrested Davis and sent him to jail first, and a Connecticut weekly credited the arrest with preventing his death.

According to the Connecticut western news, Davis, whom it called "a drunken negro," made several attempts to assault women and girls on the public streets of Stamford "last Tuesday, in broad daylight," in some cases using "the foulest language." He was arrested and taken to jail. The paper added that he "narrowly escaped being lynched" by friends of the women, who "were lying in wait for him" until the officers' "prompt arrest" intervened.
The item anticipated a trial, but no report of a trial, a grand jury action or any other outcome of the charges was found, and the next week's issue of the same paper carried no follow-up.

The episode survives in a single short item in the Connecticut western news of August 2, 1882, which gave no date beyond "last Tuesday" and did not identify the women or their friends. The paper stated the accusation as fact, called Davis "the fellow," and closed with a quip that but for the arrest "there might be a 'crowner's quest' instead of a trial." No other report of the episode, in a Connecticut paper or elsewhere, has been found.
